prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map orders the living room from the camera wearer's foreground out to the background across five frames: the seated person's grey-trousered knees, hands, and two held smartphones at the bottom-left and bottom-center are nearest at roughly 0.3–0.6 m (brightest white), immediately in front of the rectangular glass coffee table spanning ~0.7–1.5 m (light grey). On top of the glass table, a stack of books with a remote, four small snack bowls on the left, a white cup in the middle, and a tall textured vase, two teal mugs, and a small potted plant on the right sit within or just beyond arm's reach (~0.7–1.3 m), separated by ~0.5–1.0 m from the grey armchair behind the table on the left (~1.8–2.5 m) and the white TV stand, television, and tall floor plant in the right background (~2.8–3.5 m, dark grey), with windows behind them at >3.5 m (black). Across frames 1 to 5, the camera pitches slightly downward in frame 3, dips upward in frame 4, and tilts further downward and slightly rightward in frame 5, bringing the lower-left legs, both hands holding phones, and the near edge of the table higher into the frame while the upper half of the armchair and TV are cropped out of view. Compared to the RGB strip—where specular reflections and transparency on the glass tabletop obscure its surface plane—the depth map clearly renders the tabletop as a continuous tilted plane and separates the tall vase's vertical silhouette from the shelf and floor plant behind it. However, the depth map is unreliable through the glass tabletop (flattening the metal cross-frame legs underneath into the surface depth) and saturates the background windows and dark TV screen in frame 5 to near-black.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map identifies discrete scene objects and their 2D overlap layout: the grey armchair at ~1.8–2.5 m on the left is labeled 'couch', the glass coffee table in front of the viewer (~0.7–1.5 m) is labeled 'dining table', and the items arranged left-to-right across its surface (~0.1–0.3 m apart) are segmented as three to four 'bowl' instances, a 'book' with a 'remote' resting on top, a central white 'cup', a tall 'vase', two stacked/adjacent 'cup' instances, and a small 'potted plant', with a tall background 'potted plant' and 'tv' at ~2.8–3.5 m above and behind the table on the right. In the immediate foreground (~0.3–0.6 m, within arm's reach of the camera wearer and the person seated at the lower left), the person's knees and hands holding phones are partly out of view at the bottom edge, while the tall vase partially occludes the background floor plant and TV stand edge. As the camera tilts downward in frames 3 and 5 and up in frame 4, objects shift vertically in the frame and the top of the TV and armchair move out of view by frame 5. The map makes it easier than RGB alone to distinguish the individual boundaries of the clustered white bowls, cups, and overlapping remote-on-book stack on the reflective glass surface. However, the segmentation is highly unreliable on several classes and across frames: it mislabels the armchair as 'couch', the coffee table as 'dining table', and the person's grey-trousered legs at the bottom-left as 'chair' in all five frames, misses the glass tabletop entirely in frame 5, and only detects the foreground hand ('person') and right-hand smartphone ('cell phone') in frame 5.
descriptions.pose: The pose map contains no skeletons for any real person in the room, completely missing the seated person's legs, left hand holding a smartphone at the bottom-left (~0.4–0.6 m away, within arm's reach), and right hand holding a second smartphone at the bottom-center in frames 3 and 5 (~0.3–0.5 m away), all of which are cropped at the lower frame boundary and oriented away from the camera's face toward the table and screens. Instead, in all five frames, the map plots a small yellow body skeleton at ~0.8–1.0 m in the lower-left foreground where a magazine or book cover lies flat on the glass coffee table underneath the black remote. That detected figure's head keypoints sit on the left and its torso and leg segments extend downward and to the right across the book cover, facing upward/outward from the printed page rather than standing in 3D space. Across frames 1 to 5, this skeleton shifts upward and slightly leftward in frames 3 and 5 and downward in frame 4 solely due to the camera wearer's head pitch and pan, with the lower-leg keypoints partially occluded by the black remote lying directly on top of the book in frames 1 and 2. While the map highlights the presence and orientation of a human figure printed on the partially occluded magazine cover that is barely noticeable in the RGB image, it is entirely unreliable for 3D human spatial understanding because it mistakes a flat 2D print for a body and fails to detect any real body or magenta hand skeletons in the foreground.
